source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: CLAVIER is a Lockheed advisor that picks which composite part molds to cure together in an autoclave and where to put them. It matches the parts list against a library of past successful and failed loads. Case = molds, tables, 2-D positions, and outcome (valid/invalid).
numbers: Autoclave cure 6-8 h; 2 autoclaves at Sunnyvale; 2-3 loads per day; spoiled part up to $50,000; hottest and coolest part must keep within spec; ramp at least 1 degree per minute.
limits: Single site, self-reported by the builders; no controlled comparison with a no-tool baseline.
agent_relevance: A deployed CBR success was retrieval of whole past episodes with outcome labels, not a reasoning engine. Supports a case store keyed by full situation plus pass/fail label.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: Why CBR was chosen: rule-based, thermodynamic modelling and induction all failed. Experts could not explain mold placement except inside a specific past load; they reason about the load as a whole.
numbers: Machine-learning route rejected because the search space was huge and the sample of past loads only a few dozen cases. Thermodynamic model infeasible because of mold-to-mold airflow interaction.
limits: Paraphrase-level claim; the case for CBR rests on one domain where theory was missing.
agent_relevance: CBR earns its place when no causal model exists and experts reason from whole episodes. Use cases where rules cannot be written, not where a checker or spec exists.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: Timeline and cost of CLAVIER: build began March 1989, first version fielded November 1989, v1.0 done September 1990, v2.0 by November 1991, extended to Georgia in December 1992.
numbers: Development about two person-years. In daily use since September 1990. Five operators and two support staff use it. Seed cases came from the experts' own notebooks.
limits: Other sources date the start to 1987 (Aamodt & Plaza 1994; Cheetham & Watson 2006). Dates conflict between sources.
agent_relevance: Seeding the case base from existing records made a cheap start. A scaffold can seed cases from logged past solutions.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: Measured payoff: discrepancy reports from incompatible loads were 'virtually eliminated'. Each discrepancy report costs about $1000 to inspect, $2000 on average if scrapped, $20,000-$50,000 for some parts.
numbers: No before/after counts of reports, no N, no control period given. Claim is 'thousands of dollars each month'.
limits: The only outcome numbers in the primary paper are unit costs, not rates. A success rate is not reported here.
agent_relevance: Treat early success claims as anecdotal; our agent should log its own measured pass rate for retrieved cases.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: Adaptation is done by the human, then CLAVIER validates. Retriever ranks loads on 3 criteria: maximise needed parts covered, minimise extra parts, maximise compatibility. User edits; validator compares the new load to similar valid and invalid cases and predicts valid, risky, or split into two loads.
numbers: Three-way outcome: configure; suggest a similar valid alternative; strongly predicted incompatible so split the load (trading efficiency for lower risk). Removing molds from a valid load is generally compatible but molds must be repositioned.
limits: Validation is nearest-neighbour against stored negatives, not a model; the subset rule (footnote 1) is the one general principle found.
agent_relevance: Negative cases (known failures) act as a validator. Matches our G3: check a candidate against held-out evidence, here stored failures, before accepting.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: Case validity is not fixed. A load judged valid can be reclassified invalid when a similar but less risky load is found; users must be able to edit and delete cases (non-monotonic knowledge base).
numbers: Validity depends on the autoclave: same-size autoclaves with similar airflow can still differ.
limits: Close paraphrase of the text, not a direct quote.
agent_relevance: Case bases need retraction and re-labelling, not append-only. Links to the case-base maintenance subfield 07.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1995) Applying Case-Based Reasoning to Manufacturing, AI Magazine 16(1)
finding: Lessons learned: users do not care whether the system uses sophisticated AI; the interface and labour-saving features decide success. Most popular feature was printing hard copies of the loads. Input data quality limits the planner: shop data projectable only about one week.
numbers: Planner built for several weeks ahead but trustworthy only to about 1 week.
quote: Users do not care whether the application uses sophisticated AI techniques or random guesses to generate results.
limits: Authors' own reflection, not tested.
agent_relevance: Deployed value came from workflow fit and record keeping. Our agent's logging and traceability may matter as much as the retrieval.

source: Hinkle & Toomey (1994) CLAVIER, IAAI-94 proceedings
finding: Earlier conference version of the same CLAVIER paper, same abstract and same claims. Confirms the system is one of the first fielded case-based reasoning systems and the same lessons.
numbers: Text matches the 1995 AI Magazine version (same $1000, $2000, $20,000-$50,000 cost figures, same dates).
limits: Not an independent source; do not count as a replication.
agent_relevance: Two papers, one evidence base: do not count the second as independent.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches. AI Communications 7(1)
finding: Calls Lockheed's CLAVIER the first fielded CBR system. Task: optimise autoclave throughput for heat treatment of composites; knowledge lived in few experts' heads; system also helps train new staff. Says development started 1987 and regular use since fall 1990.
numbers: Handles one load in isolation; extension to sequencing several loads under test at time of writing. Strategy: low-risk, add function as experience grows.
limits: Secondary source, brief; start date (1987) differs from Hinkle & Toomey (March 1989).
agent_relevance: Gives the 4R cycle (retrieve, reuse, revise, retain) used as the frame for all deployed systems; low-risk incremental rollout is a pattern.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994), second fielded application: General Dynamics Electric Boat valve non-conformances
finding: A rule-based system for valve selection (started 1986) turned brittle and hard to maintain. A 1988 feasibility study moved to CBR; operational system fielded 1990; in use in 3 of 4 departments by fall 1991.
numbers: Rule system 5 man-years; CBR system 5 man-years (2 studies, 3 build). Total $750,000. Dec 1990 to Sep 1991: 20,000 non-conformances handled. Cost cut about 10 percent = $240,000 saved in under one year.
limits: Cost numbers as reported; no control group; the rule base was reused to structure the cases.
agent_relevance: CBR replaced rules because of brittleness and maintenance burden. Rules can seed the case base. Cost estimate is a simple before/after.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994), trends section on help desks
finding: Predicts the next wave of CBR applications will be help desks, where retrieved cases are shown as information chunks to people, not reasoned over. Notes commercial shells existed by 1992: ReMind, CBR Express/ART-IM, Esteem, CasePower.
numbers: Four shells reviewed by Harmon (1992).
limits: Prediction, borne out later by Compaq and others.
agent_relevance: Much deployed CBR is plain retrieval of past cases shown to a human. Our agent would use retrieval plus a check, not blind reuse.

source: Acorn & Walden (1992) SMART: Support Management Automated Reasoning Technology for Compaq Customer Service, IAAI-92
finding: Compaq SMART is a CBR help-desk tool (Inference's CBR Express) for support engineers. Business driver: end-user calls opened March 1991 more than doubled support requests; support staff already grew 100 percent. Justification was to retard staffing growth.
numbers: Payback of the system was one year (no dollar figure). Search 3-5 seconds; target under 2 minutes per resolution with about 5 questions answered; case base about 600 cases when first analysed.
limits: Cost model details not published in this paper; benefits claimed by the builders' own company.
agent_relevance: Deployed CBR success was measured in cost avoidance and time to answer. A scaffold's cost per solved task is the matching measure.

source: Acorn & Walden (1992) SMART: Support Management Automated Reasoning Technology for Compaq Customer Service, IAAI-92
finding: Compaq Human Factors usability study (October 1991): probability of resolving a test case was much higher with SMART.
numbers: Fewer than 50 percent of test cases resolved without SMART; 87 percent resolved with SMART. N of cases and of engineers not stated in the text.
limits: Small internal usability test; N not stated; resolution judged in the lab, not in production.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a with/without comparison in early deployed CBR: about +37 points or more. Needs N before use.

source: Acorn & Walden (1992) SMART: Support Management Automated Reasoning Technology for Compaq Customer Service, IAAI-92
finding: Case base is curated by a knowledge-engineer plus domain-expert process, with an update workflow: new cases confirmed before becoming active; automated test tools generate random text and wrong answers to find badly defined cases.
numbers: Tester can set a percentage of questions that get a wrong answer; unresolved calls escalated and then turned into new cases.
limits: Quality control is manual and costly; a case-builder style guide was needed.
agent_relevance: Gate new cases before they enter the store; stress-test retrieval with noisy and wrong inputs. Maps to a guard against poisoned memory.

source: Cheetham & Watson (2006) Fielded applications of case-based reasoning, Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3)
finding: Review of milestones. CLAVIER started 1987 in the DARPA-funding era; replaced a manual process that was already case-based; supported all 4 Rs; CBR was used as a last resort after maths models and expert systems failed; case record is only approximate shape, position and autoclave settings and ignores resin chemistry.
numbers: By 1997 over 130 major companies fielded CBR (Watson 1997). Cassiopee (Snecma, CFM56-3): goal to halve diagnosis time, meaning 25 percent less downtime, as troubleshooting is about 50 percent of downtime. ICARUS locomotive diagnosis fielded 1997.
quote: CBR was turned to only as a last resort
limits: Review by CBR proponents; no failures listed; selection bias toward successes.
agent_relevance: Fielded CBR succeeded where the task was already done by recalling past cases; fit of the method to the human process predicts success.

source: Cheetham & Watson (2006), help desks section
finding: Says SMART's CBR let technically untrained customer service staff resolve over 95 percent of calls, the rest escalated. Conversational CBR became the standard for call centres (Thomson, GE). Broderbund put a web version online at Christmas 1995 to cut support staff in the peak.
numbers: Over 95 percent of calls (review) versus 87 percent of test cases (original SMART paper). NEC SQUAD case base served 150,000 employees.
limits: The 95 percent is not in the original SMART text we read; it may be a different measure or a later figure.
agent_relevance: Conflicting numbers across secondary sources show why numbers must be traced to primary papers.

source: Cheetham (2005) Tenth Anniversary of the Plastics Color Formulation Tool, AI Magazine 26(3)
finding: GE Plastics FormTool: CBR selects a past color formula for a requested color and adapts pigment loadings. Chosen because exact physics (Kubelka-Munk) is only approximate and exhaustive colorant search needs a human to pre-pick 5-7 of 30-50 colorants. The existing process was already case-based (filing cabinets of 2,000 chips and cards).
numbers: Final formula usually 4 or 5 colorants. More than 50,000 matched colors on file; about 4,000 matches per year at start; 130 custom matches per week in 2004.
limits: Author is the builder; no external audit; savings are estimates.
agent_relevance: Another case of retrieve-then-adapt where a process was already case-based. Adaptation here was numeric and code-checked, not LLM free text.

source: Cheetham (2005) Tenth Anniversary of the Plastics Color Formulation Tool, AI Magazine 26(3)
finding: Measured benefits. Test chips needed in the revise phase fell from 4.2 to 2.7 per match, about 4.5 hours saved per match; over 5,000 matches per year gives 22,500 hours per year. Request-to-formula time cut by two thirds. Most matches took over 2 days before, now a day or less.
numbers: 1994 test: rematching 100 colours found cheaper formulas for 64 of 100. Savings $200,000 in 1994, $1.2 million 1995, $1.5 million 1996, then about $2.4 million per year estimated. First demo: one rematch saved $50,000.
limits: Before/after in one firm; confounded by other plant measures (author says savings plus other measures kept a plant open).
agent_relevance: Strongest quantified deployed-CBR record: retry count fell 36 percent (4.2 to 2.7). Retry count is a metric we can copy.

source: Cheetham (2005) Tenth Anniversary of the Plastics Color Formulation Tool, AI Magazine 26(3)
finding: Deployment lessons: build cost was two developers, under 1 year, $300,000, first for one plastic family at one site. Spreading to other sites was harder than expected because each site had a different process that had to be standardised first.
numbers: Spiral development. Globalised 1997 (English and French, central DB). Maintenance moved to IT in 1998. Four US patents. ColorXpress Select online since 1999; nine closest matches shown to customer.
limits: Single-company account.
agent_relevance: Case reuse across sites needs a shared process and a curated central store.

source: Cheetham (2005) Tenth Anniversary of the Plastics Color Formulation Tool, AI Magazine 26(3)
finding: Case retention was automatic: each saved color match is added as a new case after a filter checks it is not redundant. Case base moved from Access to Oracle, one global case base. Case selection ranks on cost and other factors, with a fuzzy preference function.
numbers: Fuzzy scale: Excellent 0.95-1, Good 0.75-0.94, Average 0.25-0.74, Poor 0-0.24.
limits: Details of the filter and similarity weights not given in this paper.
agent_relevance: Retrieval score = fit plus cost, not fit alone. Our scaffold can rank retrieved cases by fit, past pass rate and token cost; a non-redundancy filter fits memory pruning.

source: Watson lecture slides CS760 (Univ. of Auckland): CLAVIER case study
finding: Teaching summary of CLAVIER. Early version automatically substituted similar parts in a retrieved layout; engineers disliked this. CLAVIER II shows the closest layout and engineers do the substitution, then it checks the result is not similar to a known unsuccessful layout.
numbers: Slides claim: started with 20 successful layouts, hundreds later, successful layouts over 90 percent of the time. Implemented 1990, Lisp on a Mac.
limits: Slides only; the 90 percent and the 20 seed cases are not in the primary papers we read. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Auto-adapt was rejected by users; human-in-the-loop adaptation plus a negative-case check was accepted. Warning against fully automatic reuse.

source: Wikipedia, Case-based reasoning (raw wikitext checked)
finding: Names Lockheed's CLAVIER as the earliest deployed CBR system, citing Bill Mark, Case-Based Reasoning for Autoclave Management, Proceedings of the Case-Based Reasoning Workshop (1989). Also names Compaq SMART.
numbers: Primary Mark 1989 workshop paper was not located or read in this run.
limits: Mark 1989 itself not opened. The Hinkle papers thank Bill Mark for contribution to CLAVIER.
agent_relevance: Founding citation chain: Mark 1989 workshop, Hennessy & Hinkle 1992 (IEEE Expert), Hinkle & Toomey 1994/95. Only the last was read.

source: Hennessy & Hinkle (1992) Applying case-based reasoning to autoclave loading, IEEE Expert 7(5):21-26
finding: Search snippet only: describes CLAVIER structure and evaluates it as application and as a CBR research tool; says it learns as it gets new cases. Not opened (paywall).
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Not read. Do not rely on it.
agent_relevance: Gap: need this paper for the original evaluation numbers.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering
finding: Uses CBR as a RAG front end: cases are question-support-answer triples, with dual embeddings (question and support text), hybrid weights [0.25,0.40,0.35]. Case base: 2,084 cases (2,124 minus 40 removed). Test set: 32 synthetic Q/A pairs, each needing two parent cases.
numbers: Mistral-7B generator, cosine similarity to reference answer. No-RAG 0.8967. Best: hybrid AnglEBERT, k=3, full cases 0.9141, about +1.94 percent. Support-only AnglEBERT k=1 0.9121. Significant vs No-RAG and LegalBERT k=3 at 95 percent (one-tailed t-test); vs BERT k=1 at 90 percent.
limits: N=32 test items, synthetic LLM-written Q/A, embedding cosine as metric (not human or fact judged), small gains, one-tailed test, no multiple-comparison fix.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for CBR beating plain RAG: it was tested only against No-RAG. Gains are tiny.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG, retrieval analysis
finding: Retrieval F1@k over k in primes 1..37 found hybrid AnglEBERT with k=3 best. LegalBERT neighbours were more tightly clustered, so less discriminating. 57 percent of cases (1,183) had no legal-act reference.
numbers: Nearest-neighbour cosine mostly 0.7-0.8 for BERT and AnglEBERT embeddings.
limits: Same limits as above; case bank built from the same corpus that made the test items.
agent_relevance: Embedding choice and case representation changed results more than the CBR label did; test representations, not just k.

source: Das et al. (2021/2022) Case-Based Reasoning for Natural Language Queries over Knowledge Bases (CBR-KBQA), EMNLP
finding: Neuro-symbolic CBR: retrieve similar questions and their logical forms, generate a new logical form reusing parts, then a revise step aligns relations to the KB neighbourhood. Beats a same-size T5-11B baseline on compositional questions.
numbers: ComplexWebQuestions hidden test strict accuracy: T5-11B 52.4, T5+revise 55.6, CBR-KBQA 67.1 (leaderboard 70.4 under lenient scoring). CFQ: MCD1 72.9 to 87.8, MCD2 69.2 to 75.1, MCD3 62.0 to 71.5.
limits: Pre-LLM trained seq2seq (not a prompted LLM). Needs labelled question-program pairs. Authors claim 11 percent over prior state of the art on CWQ.
agent_relevance: A real gain from reusing parts of several retrieved cases for novel combinations. The revise step helped (about +3 F1 points on CWQ).

source: Atzeni et al. (2022) Case-Based Reasoning for Better Generalization in Textual Reinforcement Learning, ICLR
finding: CBR memory of past positive-reward situations improves text-game agents, mainly out of distribution. Retrieval by learned context similarity; vector quantisation beat locality-sensitive hashing.
numbers: TextWorld Commonsense hard level out-of-distribution: average drop 6 percent with CBR versus 35 percent without. Jericho: better or comparable scores on 24 of 33 games (73 percent).
limits: Small RL agents, not LLM prompts; text games; compared with older baselines.
agent_relevance: Memory of successful episodes protects against distribution shift; supports reuse of past successes for new tasks.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) Case-Based Reasoning with Language Models for Classification of Logical Fallacies, IJCAI
finding: CBR with BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA: retrieve similar fallacy cases and adapt, with enriched case representations (goals, explanations, counterarguments, structure). CBR beats vanilla models by 2.5-6 absolute F1 in domain, up to 8 out of domain (LOGIC Climate), and beats few-shot Codex.
numbers: Case representation changes F1 by 6-8 points in domain, 4-8 out of domain. Counterarguments best; generic explanations hurt. Best at k=1 with only 10 percent of the case base; larger case bases lowered scores. Retrieved cases' labels agree with truth only 27.7 percent of the time.
quote: Having access to too much data makes the model dependent and sensitive to the unnecessary and insignificant details
limits: Small fine-tuned encoders, 13 fallacy classes, augmented to 281 args per class; not a prompted frontier LLM.
agent_relevance: Less can be better: a small curated case set beat the full one. Do not use retrieved labels blindly; they act indirectly.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Casts agent learning as memory-based case retrieval (Memory-augmented MDP): store (state, action, reward) cases, retrieve with a learned or similarity policy, no gradient updates. Planner GPT-4.1, executor o3/o4-mini.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88 Pass@3 (top-1 on 26 June 2025 board); test 79.40. DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM. SimpleQA 95.0. Case memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 absolute points out of distribution.
limits: Pass@3 on validation with a case bank built over 3 iterations on that same validation set; test used that bank. Selection effects and leakage risk. Authors' self-report.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence for case memory in an LLM agent; our G3 asks whether cases were fitted to the test items.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento ablations
finding: Number of retrieved cases K barely matters beyond a few. DeepResearcher average F1/PM: K=0 59.9/72.2; K=1 63.6/77.9; K=4 64.5/78.5 (best); K=32 63.9/78.1. Learning curve over 5 iterations: no CBR 78.65 to 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85; parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44.
numbers: HLE average F1/PM: Memento without CBR 22.2/17.4; Memento 26.7/24.4. SimpleQA 81.0/89.7 to 84.7/95.0.
quote: CBR benefits from a small, high-quality memory, unlike few-shot prompting
limits: CBR gain over the same agent without cases is small on in-distribution sets (about 0.4 to 0.9 points at iteration 5); iteration count is itself a big factor (about +6 points without CBR).
agent_relevance: Most improvement came from repeated iterations and tools; case memory gave a smaller increment. Keep K small (1-4).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners, AAAI
finding: Agent stores successful trajectories and retrieves by task similarity as in-context examples, plus extracts text insights. Retrieval by task similarity beat reasoning-similarity retrieval, which beat random sampling in ALFWorld.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36 vs 31 percent, ALFWorld 50 vs 55 percent. HotpotQA ExpeL 40 percent at R3 vs Reflexion 39; ALFWorld ExpeL 59 vs Reflexion 54. Four-fold validation.
limits: Closely related to CBR but does not call itself CBR; gpt-3.5/gpt-4 era; small N per environment.
agent_relevance: Which memory is best depends on the task: general rules for reasoning (HotpotQA), concrete trajectories for action tasks (ALFWorld). Pick by task type.

source: Deployed-CBR synthesis across sources opened in this run
finding: Across CLAVIER, Electric Boat, SMART, FormTool: success came when (1) a human process already recalled past cases, (2) rules or physics models had failed or been too brittle, (3) outcomes were labelled, (4) humans did adaptation, and (5) the case base was curated.
numbers: FormTool 4.2 to 2.7 chips (-36 percent) and $2.4M/yr; Electric Boat about 10 percent, $240K in under a year; SMART 87 vs under 50 percent resolved (lab test); CLAVIER discrepancy reports virtually eliminated (no count).
limits: All outcomes builder-reported, no randomised control, no failed deployments reported (publication bias).
agent_relevance: Scaffold rule candidates: label outcomes, store failures, human or code-checked adaptation, curated small case set, measure retries. Check against SCHEMA G2 and G3 before adding.
